# Bug 1606176 - EffectSet cascade information access should be audited.

## Basic Information
- **Status**: NEW
- **Severity**: S3
- **Product**: Core
- **Component**: CSS Transitions and Animations
- **Version**: unspecified
- **Platform**: Unspecified
- **OS**: Unspecified
- **Created**: 2019-12-27T23:34:40Z
- **Last Updated**: 2022-10-11T23:47:31Z

## People Involved
- **Reporter**: Emilio Cobos Álvarez [:emilio] (emilio@crisal.io)
- **Assignee**: Nobody; OK to take it and work on it (nobody@mozilla.org)
- **CC Count**: 6 people

## Bug Relationships
- **Depends on**: 1605610

## Bug Timeline

**2019-12-27 23:34:40** - Comment #0 by emilio@crisal.io
The mechanisms introduced in bug 1228229 / bug 1339704 are flawed. At least the usage in `ComposeSortedEffects`.

Usage of `EffectSet::PropertiesForAnimationsLevel` is clearly wrong from `ComposeSortedEffects`, as that makes us rely on information that isn't updated when you do stuff like `GetComputedStyleNoFlush` (see bug 1605610 for a particularly terrible consequence of it).

In bug 1605610 I'm fixing the check so that at least it doesn't make us create bogus transitions, by filtering animations by the cascade level (which seems like the obvious thing to do anyway).

If I do that, only a few tests fail, in particular `Animation overrides/stops overriding transition immediately` and such. Which expects an animation to apply even though a transition is overriding it in the cascade.

I am confused, is that test correct? Shouldn't running transitions always win per https://drafts.csswg.org/css-cascade/#cascading-origins?

IIUC `!important` rules should win over animations (and other browsers don't do that). But I wasn't aware that animations should override transitions... What's the deal with that?

---

**2019-12-27 23:53:46** - Comment #1 by emilio@crisal.io
Ok, I found that bit in https://drafts.csswg.org/css-transitions/#application (that is pretty weird btw...).

Anyhow, we still need to figure out what to do with it.

---

**2019-12-28 02:31:53** - Comment #2 by emilio@crisal.io
Ok, so I did a bit more digging about why bug 1605610 happens, and I _think_ the initial styling may be the only problematic case here (but please double-check me).

In particular, what happens there is that `StyleNewSubtree()` only calls `PreTraverseInSubtree` _after_ styling the nodes, and not before. That's ok for pseudo-elements and other stuff that can't have programmatic animations.

But if we hit [this call of `StyleNewSubtree`](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/723e61e5f6fe36e69592b7742bc10338392e53e4/layout/base/nsCSSFrameConstructor.cpp#2158), the one that I was trying to remove in that bug initially (I'll move that to another bug), then we hit the broken case on initial styling and create the bogus transition rule that we then never remove. After that, then we'd update the cascade effects in the animation tasks.

So it _might_ be the case that with that patch that prevents the bogus transition rule which we never remove, we are done and we have correct behavior...

---

**2019-12-30 00:34:59** - Comment #3 by hikezoe.birchill@mozilla.com
As you've already noticed, the test cases you mentioned in comment 0 are correct test cases I believe.

I don't still follow about comment 2, I assume I need to understand what's going on the case in bug 1605610.

---

**2020-01-06 01:57:19** - Comment #4 by brian@birchill.co.jp
Canceling ni here because it seems like you found the answer as per comment 1. I can't comment on the rationale behind that condition since it predates my involvement in the spec.

---

**2020-01-09 05:25:43** - Comment #5 by boris.chiou@gmail.com
(In reply to Emilio Cobos Álvarez (:emilio) from comment #0)
> If I do that, only a few tests fail, in particular `Animation overrides/stops overriding transition immediately` and such. Which expects an animation to apply even though a transition is overriding it in the cascade.
> 
> I am confused, is that test correct? Shouldn't running transitions always win per https://drafts.csswg.org/css-cascade/#cascading-origins?
> 
> IIUC `!important` rules should win over animations (and other browsers don't do that). But I wasn't aware that animations should override transitions... What's the deal with that?

Sorry for my late reply. Actually I have the same question when working on this. I believe other engines do the same thing, right? Comment 1 addresses this, and perhaps we can raise this question during F2F? Maybe dbaron or other google guys know why we have this kind of design.

---

**2020-01-09 06:01:30** - Comment #6 by dbaron@dbaron.org
The [Application of transitions](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-transitions-1/#application) section of the spec says:

> Implementations must add this value to the cascade if and only if that property is not currently undergoing a CSS Animation ([CSS3-ANIMATIONS]) on the same element.

(It's done this way because essentially the goal was to have a circular set of priorities!)

---

**2020-01-09 06:06:28** - Comment #7 by dbaron@dbaron.org
Basically, I think the reasoning is:

1. transitions should override everything, since they're only triggered by things that can be computed values, so you're guaranteed to be transitioning between things that were the results of the cascade, and it's easiest if they just override everything (for implementations) and it also means they work the highest portion of the time (no matter where the computed value comes from)

2. `!important` rules should be able to override animations, because users should have overall control (for various reasons, including accessibility)

3. animations should override transitions when both are running, because animations show a clearer intent to animate in a particular way.  (I don't think I'm expressing this one all that well -- I might recall more if I dug in to the history of this part.  Birtles also might remember more -- it's the most recent of the three.)

---

**2020-01-09 07:58:50** - Comment #8 by brian@birchill.co.jp
(In reply to David Baron :dbaron: 🏴󠁵󠁳󠁣󠁡󠁿 ⌚UTC-8 from comment #7)
> 3. animations should override transitions when both are running, because animations show a clearer intent to animate in a particular way.  (I don't think I'm expressing this one all that well -- I might recall more if I dug in to the history of this part.  Birtles also might remember more -- it's the most recent of the three.)

Unfortunately I don't remember the rationale about this. I thought it pre-dated my involvement in the spec but the reason you mention does sound familiar.

That said, given that at least Blink, Edge, and Gecko (I haven't tested WebKit) support this behavior I wonder how likely it is to be something we'd change.

---

**2020-01-13 12:05:56** - Comment #9 by release-mgmt-account-bot@mozilla.tld
The priority flag is not set for this bug.
:mats, could you have a look please?

For more information, please visit [auto_nag documentation](https://wiki.mozilla.org/Release_Management/autonag#workflow.2Fno_priority.py).

---

**2020-01-13 13:13:35** - Changes by emilio@crisal.io
  - priority: '--' → 'P3'

---

**2022-10-11 23:47:31** - Changes by [Redacted]
  - severity: '[Filtered]' → '[Filtered]'
